other.about: Surface envelope and tectonic regimes (S0; surface design sections 1, 2.1 and 6): which kind of surface a world has at each date, why, and the cheap sketch globe for unexamined and scanned worlds. Rules are tried in order; the first whose conditions all hold names the regime.

rules.because: the gas envelope is the planet: there is no solid surface to reach
the heat of formation keeps the surface molten
the surface is hotter than rock's melting point
too small for gravity to overcome the strength of its rock or ice and pull it round: a shape of lumps and craters
cold enough for methane rain under a thick atmosphere, on a crust of water ice
so much water that no land rises above it
so much water that no land rises above it
a water-rich world too cold for open sea, its ice shell thin enough for tidal cracks to cross it: the shell breaks and renews its surface
a water-rich world too cold for open sea, its ice shell too thick for cracks to cross: a rigid lid that keeps its craters
heat flow so high it escapes through constant eruption rather than conduction
carbon outnumbers oxygen in its building blocks: graphite and carbide crust
a super-Earth with enough heat for plates or a stagnant lid; research is divided
heat flow above the critical value and surface water to weaken the lid, so the crust breaks into moving plates
enough heat for plates but too dry: the lid holds, then fails in global resurfacing
one global plate: too small, too cool or too quiet for the lid to break

sources.q_crit_w_m2: the base-physics atom sse.heat.active_geology_lifetime uses the same threshold
sources.tide: despinning time and tidal heating after Gladman et al. 1996, Icarus 122, 166 (doi:10.1006/icar.1996.0117) and Peale and Cassen 1978; Q 100 and k2 0.3 are rocky-world defaults
sources.greenhouse_k: Earth's present greenhouse warming is about 33 K; applied only when a generated world has volatiles (oceans or CO2), until an atmosphere stage exists
sources.atlas: surfaces research report section 3: cube-sphere quadtree, level 0 about 20 km per sample on an Earth (here level 1 at 256 samples per tile), fact floor about 100 m anywhere and 10 m in declared sites; detail octaves fall off with a Hurst exponent of 0.8, typical of planetary topography (Turcotte 1987; Rosenburg et al. 2015 for the Moon)
sources.plates: semi-Lagrangian kinematic plates on the cube grid in the spirit of Cortial et al. 2019 (Procedural Tectonic Planets, Computer Graphics Forum 38, 2. doi:10.1111/cgf.13614); plate speeds of a few cm/yr scaled by heat flow; sea-floor depth from crust age by the GDH1 plate model (Stein and Stein 1992, Nature 359, 123. doi:10.1038/359123a0); continental elevation by Airy isostasy (factor (rho_m - rho_c)/rho_m, about 0.18); mountain belts worn down with an e-folding time of about 150 Myr (Pinet and Souriau 1988)
sources.wear: stream-power incision E = K Q^m S solved implicitly in drainage order (Braun and Willett 2013, Geomorphology 180, 170. doi:10.1016/j.geomorph.2012.10.008); depression filling by priority-flood (Barnes et al. 2014, Computers and Geosciences 62, 117. doi:10.1016/j.cageo.2013.04.024); Hack's law L ~ A^0.6 (Hack 1957) as the drainage check; diffusion is an effective coarse-grid value (the local hillslope value is about 0.01 m2/yr); runoff, glaciers (ice balance) and dunes (saltation and dryness, Lancaster's mobility index at least 0.5) from the one climate's water and wind at each cell's height (W9)
sources.impacts: chronology after Neukum, Ivanov and Hartmann 2001 (doi:10.1023/A:1011989004263); production slopes -3 below 1 km and -2 above (Hartmann-type); saturation 0.15 D^-2 per km2, about 10% of geometric saturation (1.54 D^-2), the top of the 1-10% range of Gault 1970 (Radio Science 5, 273); Hartmann 1984 (doi:10.1016/0019-1035(84)90138-6) finds a shallower D^-1.83 equilibrium; documented fudge (docs/fudges.md); crater size scales as g^-0.216 (Holsapple 1993, doi:10.1146/annurev.ea.21.050193.002001); depth and rim after Pike 1977, transitions 15, 150 and 600 km at lunar gravity scaled as 1/g (Melosh 1989); atmosphere cut-off 0.1 km x P^0.75 fitted to Earth and Venus (no Venus craters under about 3 km); dry degradation 5.5 m2/Myr (Fassett and Thomson 2014, doi:10.1002/2014JE004698), wet 5e4 m2/Myr set so a 10 km crater on a wet world loses most of its relief in about 100 Myr; renewal times: Europa about 60 Myr (Schenk et al. 2004, in Jupiter: The Planet, Satellites and Magnetosphere, ch. 18, from the cratering rates of Zahnle et al. 2003, doi:10.1016/S0019-1035(03)00048-4), Venus about 500 Myr, Titan about 500 Myr, Io under 1 Myr; volcanism thresholds, plains rates and shield growth are rule-of-thumb values for lid worlds (Mars, Moon, Mercury), labelled as such; shields reach 9 km x (9.81/g); renewal rates scale as the cube of heat flow against each regime's reference (so a cooling Ganymede keeps its younger craters while Europa keeps none); shields need a lid world of at least 3000 km radius (none on the Moon or Mercury)
sources.cover: S7 cover: temperature, wetness and prevailing winds from the one climate (W7a, packs/base-climate: North 1975 energy balance, Held and Hou 1980, Rhines 1975); moist lapse about 6.5 K/km against 9.8 dry; 0.1 bar tropopause (Robinson and Catling 2014, Nature Geoscience 7, 12. doi:10.1038/ngeo2020); ice thresholds tuned so Earth's equatorial snow line sits near 5 km and land ice starts near 65° (to measure on more worlds)
sources.features: S7 features: read from the atlas's own level-0 tiles; ranges are land 1.5 standard deviations above the mean land height; names from a neutral syllable set

ice-shell.source: tidal flexing cracks the shell and ridges grow either side (Kattenhorn and Hurford 2009, in Europa, 199; Europa's lineae trend about 45 degrees from east).
the shell pulled apart and new ice filled the gap (Prockter et al. 2002, JGR 107, 5028. doi:10.1029/2000JE001458).
warm ice or melt below broke the shell into rafts (Schmidt et al. 2011, Nature 479, 502. doi:10.1038/nature10608); cover follows today's heat flow.

heat-pipe.source: a volcanic depression over a magma column; Io has about 417 (Radebaugh et al. 2001, JGR 106, 33005. doi:10.1029/2000JE001406).
a crustal block thrust up as buried lava sinks and compresses the lithosphere (Turtle et al. 2001, JGR 106, 33175. doi:10.1029/2000JE001354; about 135 on Io).

episodic-lid.source: an upwelling plume domed and fractured the lid; Venus has several hundred, 60 to over 2000 km across (Stofan et al. 1992, JGR 97, 13347. doi:10.1029/92JE01314).
a rift belt where the lid stretched (Venus's chasmata).
older deformed highland crust that escaped the last overturn (about 8% of Venus).

plume-lid.source: plumes dome a weak lid (Lourenco et al. 2020).
a rift belt where the lid stretched.

stagnant-lid.source: a thrust fault as the cooling world shrank (lobate scarps; Byrne et al. 2014, Nature Geosci. 7, 301. doi:10.1038/ngeo2097); height scales with radius.

hydrocarbon.source: organic sand blown into linear dunes by the winds near the equator (Lorenz et al. 2006, Science 312, 724. doi:10.1126/science.1123257).
methane and ethane collect near the poles, mostly in the north (Hayes 2016).

carbon-rich.source: speculative: pooled hydrocarbons on a carbon-rich crust (Kuchner and Seager 2005).

clouds.source: jets from the Rhines scale (Rhines 1975, J. Fluid Mech. 69, 417. doi:10.1017/S0022112075001504) with empirical wind scales: gas giants about 150 m/s, ice giants about 400 m/s; cloud chemistry by 1-bar temperature, adapted from the effective-temperature classes of Sudarsky et al. 2000 (ApJ 538, 885. doi:10.1086/309160: ammonia below about 150 K Teff, water, clear, alkali 900 to 1500 K, silicate above); the thresholds here are on the 1-bar temperature, the clear class is not modelled and the methane-ice row is an ice-giant addition (docs/fudges.md)

deposits.copper-arc: porphyry copper forms above subduction arcs and is mostly found in young arcs because erosion removes it (Kesler and Wilkinson 2008, Geology 36, 255. doi:10.1130/G24317A.1)
deposits.gold-orogenic: orogenic gold is deposited by fluids driven out during collisions, in old mountain belts (Goldfarb et al. 2001, Ore Geology Reviews 18, 1. doi:10.1016/S0169-1368(01)00016-6)
deposits.nickel-flood: magmatic nickel-copper sulphides form in flood-basalt feeders such as Noril'sk (Naldrett 1999, Mineralium Deposita 34, 227. doi:10.1007/s001260050200)
deposits.nickel-impact: the Sudbury nickel ores settled out of an impact melt sheet (Lightfoot 2017, Nickel Sulfide Ores and Impact Melts, Elsevier. doi:10.1016/C2014-0-02315-6)
deposits.carbon-buried: coal and oil form where life's remains are buried quickly in thick sediment
deposits.ice-shadowed: permanently shadowed polar craters trap water ice (Watson, Murray and Brown 1961, JGR 66, 3033. doi:10.1029/JZ066i009p03033; confirmed at Mercury by Lawrence et al. 2013, Science 339, 292. doi:10.1126/science.1229953)

aerostat.source: band: about Earth sea-level pressure and 0 to 50 °C, where a breathable-gas envelope floats in heavier air (Landis 2003, AIP Conf. Proc. 654, 1193. doi:10.1063/1.1541418); drift wind 60 m/s is Venus's cloud-level super-rotation order (Sánchez-Lavega et al. 2017, Space Science Reviews 212, 1541. doi:10.1007/s11214-017-0389-x), a default until a weather stage gives winds

built.source: settlements favour fresh water, mild climate, flat low ground and coasts
ports sit on coasts that are not frozen
mines go where the deposits are
a base on an airless or hostile world wants flat ground, low and near the equator (easier landings and launches)

naming.source: a neutral syllable set; a universe or culture pack replaces it with its own naming rules
